top_choice_rationale: P003 (Persson, Tabellini, Besley) is a mature programme of about three decades that made the policy outcomes of political systems an object of formal analysis and evidence. It links electoral rules, constitutional form, accountability and state capacity to taxation, spending and public-goods provision, and it has been extended and taught widely in public economics, development and political economy. A citation limited to rules, state capacity and fiscal outcomes is distinct from the 2024 prize on the historical origins of institutions. I hold this first place narrowly. Identification of constitutional effects is weaker than in design-based work, credit between the Persson-Tabellini and Besley-Persson strands is not cleanly separable, and the first-place support for P003 is not independent evidence. P002 (Grossman-Helpman) is a close second, with the cleanest two-person attribution but a mixed empirical record. P001 (Helpman-Melitz) has the widest footprint in data and estimation but an unresolved credit boundary with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum. P004 has the most credible designs, but the persistence and shift-share debates and the task-framework attribution questions remain. A prize this year is preferable to no award.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile. I overlapped with Hassler and Krusell at Stockholm University in 2010-17, an institutional overlap and not a co-authorship, and both also prefer P003. My Uppsala and IFAU co-authors are not credited on any shortlisted item. My labour-economics interests are adjacent to P004. Colleagues recall institutional proximity between some P003 candidates and committee members. My profile does not document this, and I have not verified it.
